lead: The command line is a text loop. The shell prints a prompt, you type one line, the shell runs it, prints the result, and the prompt returns. The same line always does the same thing, and a line saved in a file can be run again tomorrow. That is why servers and cloud machines are run from a terminal: exact, scriptable, cheap over a slow ssh link. This chapter shows the loop, the shape of a command, and the commands for moving around directories and looking after files.
prereq: You need: the kernel/shell split from Chapter 1.3 and the idea of a login session from Chapter 1.5.

sections.h3: The prompt loop and the shape of a command

blocks.text: Open a terminal and the shell prints a prompt and waits. A typical prompt is ravi@laptop:~$ — user name, machine name, current directory, then a $ sign. A $ means an ordinary user; a # means root. You type a line and press Enter. The shell splits the line into words, finds the program named by the first word, runs it, shows its output, and prints the prompt again.

Every line has the same shape. The command is a program name and must come first. Options change how the command behaves; short options start with one hyphen (-l) and long options with two (--all). Arguments are the things the command acts on, usually file or directory names. Spaces separate the words. Case matters: ls works, LS does not. So ls -la /tmp means: run ls, with combined options -l and -a, on the directory /tmp.

blocks.where: command is the program name; options are flags such as -l or --all; arguments are file names, directory names or other words the command needs. Square brackets mean optional.

blocks.text: Words are exact and repeatable. The same line gives the same result, and a line can be stored in a file and replayed. It also survives a slow link, which is why remote servers are managed this way.

sections.h3: Moving around and listing: pwd, cd, mkdir, rmdir, ls

blocks.text: pwd prints the absolute path of the current directory, that is, the full path starting from the root /. cd changes that directory: cd notes enters a subdirectory, cd /home/ravi goes to an absolute path, cd .. goes to the parent, cd with no argument goes to your home directory, and cd - returns to the previous directory. mkdir notes creates a directory. mkdir -p a/b/c creates the whole chain and does not complain if part already exists. rmdir removes a directory only when it is empty.

ls lists the names in a directory. ls -a also shows names beginning with a dot, which are hidden by default, plus . (this directory) and .. (the parent). ls -l prints one long line per entry. Combine them as ls -la.

blocks.text: cat a.txt prints the whole file to the screen; it suits short files. more a.txt shows one screen and waits for the space bar. less a.txt does the same but scrolls both ways, and q quits. lpr a.txt sends the file to the printer queue, so printing from a terminal needs no application.

cp a.txt b.txt copies the contents into b.txt. Add -r to copy a whole directory. mv a.txt /tmp/work/ moves the file; mv a.txt c.txt renames it in place. rm a.txt deletes a file, and rm -r notes deletes a directory with everything inside it. ln a.txt hard makes a hard link, a second name for the same file; ln -s /home/ravi/a.txt shortcut makes a symbolic link, a small file that points at the target. find /home/ravi -name "*.txt" walks the tree and prints matching paths.

chmod changes permissions in one line: chmod u+x run.sh adds execute for the owner, and chmod 644 a.txt gives the owner read and write, everyone else read. Permission bits, owners and groups are covered properly in Unit 2.

sections.h3: The vi editor and getting help

blocks.text: vi a.txt opens a file and creates it on the first save. vi has modes. You start in command mode, where keys are commands, not text. Press i to enter insert mode and type your line. Press Esc to return to command mode. Then :w writes to disk, :q quits, :wq writes and quits, and :q! quits and throws the changes away.

items: Type vi a.txt and press Enter.
Press i, type the text, and press Enter for a new line.
Press Esc to leave insert mode.
Type :wq and press Enter to save and exit.
To abandon the edit instead, type :q! and press Enter.

blocks.text: For help, man ls shows the manual page for ls; space pages forward and q quits. Manual pages are grouped in numbered sections: section 1 is user commands, section 5 is file formats, section 8 is administration commands, so man 5 passwd reads the file format rather than the command. man -k word searches the one-line descriptions. Most GNU commands also accept --help, a short summary that is faster when you need one option.

figure.caption: The seven typed commands in order, with the two printed outputs. After rm a.txt, notes holds only b.txt and the shell stays in /home/ravi/notes.

examples.question: A user logs in and the shell starts in /home/ravi. These commands are typed in order: (1) mkdir notes, (2) cd notes, (3) pwd, (4) vi a.txt, where one line is typed and the file is saved and closed with :wq, (5) cp a.txt b.txt, (6) ls, (7) rm a.txt. Give (a) the output of pwd, (b) the output of ls, (c) the final working directory, and (d) the files left inside notes. (6 marks)
steps: mkdir notes creates an empty directory named notes inside /home/ravi. No output is printed.
cd notes moves the shell's own working directory into that new directory, so the shell is now at /home/ravi/notes.
pwd prints the absolute path of that directory: /home/ravi/notes.
vi a.txt starts an editor session. The typed line is held in the editor's buffer; :wq writes it to a.txt and exits. notes now contains a.txt.
cp a.txt b.txt reads a.txt and writes an identical b.txt, so notes contains two files: a.txt and b.txt.
ls prints the two names in the current directory, in sorted order: a.txt and b.txt (shown in columns on a terminal, one per line when piped).
rm a.txt unlinks a.txt. The directory now holds only b.txt and the shell stays where it is.
examples.answer: pwd prints /home/ravi/notes; ls prints a.txt and b.txt; the final working directory is /home/ravi/notes; only b.txt is left in notes.

traps: rm does not use a trash folder. A deleted file is gone, and rm -r on the wrong directory can remove a whole tree with no undo.
rmdir refuses a directory that still has entries in it; the error is 'Directory not empty', not a permissions problem.
cd changes only the working directory of the shell process that runs it. A script that runs cd cannot move the terminal you launched it from, because the script is a child process with its own copy.
mv inside one file system just renames the entry and the file keeps its identity; cp makes a new file with a new identity. mv across file systems has to copy and then delete.

ls without -a hides every name beginning with a dot, so a 'missing' file may simply be hidden. Quote the pattern, as in find /home/ravi -name "*.txt", so the shell passes it unchanged to find. Unquoted, the shell may expand *.txt into matching file names in the current directory before find ever sees it.

quiz.q: What do the prompt endings $ and # tell you?
quiz.a: $ means an ordinary user is logged in; # means the root user, who can change anything.

quiz.q: A script contains cd /tmp. Why does the terminal you ran it from stay in its old directory?
quiz.a: The script runs as a child process. It gets its own copy of the working directory, so its cd affects only itself; the parent shell's directory is unchanged.

quiz.q: In a directory holding a.txt, .hidden and b.txt, what does ls print, what does ls -a print, and how many lines does ls -l print?
quiz.a: ls prints a.txt and b.txt. ls -a prints ., .., .hidden, a.txt, b.txt. ls -l prints a 'total' line plus two entry lines, one each for a.txt and b.txt (.hidden stays hidden without -a).

quiz.q: Break the line ls -la /tmp into command, options and arguments.
quiz.a: Command: ls. Options: -l and -a, written together as -la. Argument: /tmp.

quiz.q: A student runs rmdir notes and gets 'Directory not empty'. Give two ways to finish the job and say which is riskier.
quiz.a: Either delete the contents first (cd notes; rm the files; cd ..; rmdir notes), or run rm -r notes. The second is riskier: one typing slip removes the wrong tree with no undo, so check the path with pwd and ls first.

quiz.q: Which key takes vi from insert mode back to command mode, and which command saves and quits?
quiz.a: Esc returns to command mode; :wq writes the file and quits.

quiz.q: How does :q! differ from :wq, and when would each be used?
quiz.a: :wq saves the buffer to disk then exits, used when the edit is wanted. :q! exits without saving, used to throw away a bad edit. Plain :q refuses to exit if there are unsaved changes.

quiz.q: You need the option that makes ls sort by modification time. Which help route gives it fastest, and why?
quiz.a: ls --help prints the option summary on one screen, so the flag (-t) is found fast. man ls is complete but long; man -k ls would search descriptions rather than the options of ls itself.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the same loop runs inside ssh sessions, Docker containers and CI jobs, where no desktop exists and every step must be a repeatable line. Tools such as tmux keep a session alive after the network drops. Next, read about manual page sections and POSIX conventions for utility options, then how a shell stores command history in ~/.bash_history.
